Wildlife walks notice
The wildlife walks team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the woodland trails session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the wildlife walks may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The young naturalists meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one woodland trails guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from coding clubs, digital skills and online safety courses. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: After-school app building club for Year 7 to 9 — If your child has ever said "I wish I could make my own app," this is the place to start. Over ten Thursday afternoons, students design, code and test a simple mobile app using a visual programming tool. No prior coding knowledge is required. Each student finishes with a working app they can show friends. Laptops are provided; just bring ideas.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Saturday robotics lab for teenagers — Every Saturday from ten to twelve, teenagers build and programme small robots in a fully equipped lab. Sessions progress from basic motor control to sensor-based navigation and line-following challenges. Teams of three compete in a mini tournament at the end of each term. The lab holds twelve participants, so booking ahead is essential.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Online safety workshop for parents and carers — Practical and jargon-free, this two-hour evening session helps adults understand the apps, games and social platforms their children use. A safeguarding officer demonstrates privacy settings, explains grooming warning signs and shows how to set up parental controls. Attendees leave with a printed family agreement template. Free for school families.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Weekend game design jam at the library — In the community room above Harborough Library, young people aged twelve to sixteen spend a full Saturday creating a computer game from scratch. Mentors from a local studio guide each team through storyboarding, pixel art and basic scripting. Pizza is provided, and every team presents their game at four p.m. Entry is five pounds.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Digital photography and editing masterclass — After three Sunday sessions, participants will have a portfolio of ten edited photographs and the skills to shoot in manual mode. A professional photographer covers composition, lighting and free editing software. Bring any camera with manual settings, including older models. The final session includes a group exhibition at the community centre.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Lunchtime podcast recording club — Fancy hearing your voice on a real podcast? Join a small group of students who plan, record and publish a weekly episode about school life. Meetings are every Tuesday at lunch in the media room. You can present, operate the microphone, or edit audio — all roles are welcome. Episodes go live on the school website every Friday.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Coding bootcamp for career changers — Stuck in a job with no prospects? This intensive twelve-week evening bootcamp teaches web development from HTML to JavaScript. No degree or technical background is needed. A careers adviser helps with CV writing and interview prep in the final fortnight. Payment plans spread the cost over six months. Graduates join an alumni network for job leads.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Senior citizens tablet and smartphone clinic — Older adults who feel left behind by technology can drop into this patient, friendly clinic every Monday and Thursday morning. Volunteers help with video calls, online shopping, NHS appointments and photo sharing. No question is too basic, and sessions last as long as needed. Bring your own device; chargers and large-print guides are available.

questions.prompt: Ravi is fourteen and wants to build robots with friends on Saturday mornings. He enjoys competition and does not mind committing to a full term.
Mrs Thompson is seventy and struggles to video-call her grandchildren. She wants a relaxed morning session where she can ask basic questions without feeling rushed.
Jake is twelve and dreams of making his own mobile game. He is free on Thursdays after school and has never written code before.
Sandra is a mother of two teenagers and worries about their online safety. She wants a practical evening talk that shows her how to set up controls and spot risks.
Omar is thirty-five and wants to leave his warehouse job for a tech career. He can study in the evenings and needs help with interviews and CVs.

passage.text: When the young naturalists in our town started a wildlife walks project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving woodland trails. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

passage.text: The old community centre in our area had been closed for years, and the building was falling apart. (16) ..... A group of residents decided it was time to bring it back to life and create a space where everyone could meet and socialise. The building had been a popular meeting place in the past, but after it closed, people had nowhere to go for social activities, and many residents felt the area had lost its heart.

We formed a committee and applied for a grant from the local council to cover the cost of materials. (17) ..... To our surprise, the application was approved within a month, and we received enough funding to start the renovation work. We organised fundraising events such as cake sales and sponsored walks to raise extra money, and the local community responded generously to our appeals for help.

The renovation work began on a Saturday morning, with volunteers of all ages taking part. (18) ..... Some people painted walls, while others repaired the broken windows and doors, and everyone worked together despite having different skills. The younger volunteers cleaned the garden area at the back, cutting down overgrown bushes and planting new flowers to create a pleasant outdoor space for everyone to enjoy.

The biggest challenge was the old kitchen, which needed new plumbing and electrical wiring throughout. (19) ..... A local plumber offered to do the work at a reduced rate because he believed in the project and wanted to support the community. He spent three weekends installing the new kitchen, working long hours without complaining, and his contribution saved the project thousands of pounds for other improvements.

After six months of hard work by everyone involved, the centre finally reopened. (20) ..... It now hosts art classes, youth clubs and weekly coffee mornings for elderly residents who live alone. The reopening ceremony was attended by over a hundred people, including the mayor, and the event was covered by the local television news channel that evening.

A local café provided free drinks for (24) ..... the volunteers as a thank-you gesture for their hard work.
